articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License FF, Extending Wind-Down Period for Iraq Development Bank
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran-related General License (GL) FF-1, which replaces and supersedes GL FF. This amendment extends the authorization for transactions necessary to wind down dealings involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, also known as Iraq Development Bank, and any entity in which it owns, directly or indirectly, a 50 percent or greater interest.

The wind-down period has been extended from October 30, 2026, to December 1, 2026. The updated license, effective October 29, 2026, also stipulates that payments to blocked persons must be made into blocked accounts.
This action is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to manage sanctions against Iran, while providing specific authorizations for certain transactions.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entity Supporting North Korean IT Worker Schemes and Sanctions Rwandan Entities for DRC Destabilization
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctioned ten individuals and one entity for their involvement in North Korean government-run information technology (IT) worker schemes. These schemes allegedly defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for North Korea's illicit weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missile programs.

The designations target facilitators and IT workers based in North Korea and Russia, including a Russian intermediary who conducted nearly $2 million in cryptocurrency conversions for DPRK officials. North Korean IT workers reportedly use forged documents and stolen identities to secure employment, exploiting access to systems to exfiltrate data and intellectual property, with most wages confiscated by the regime.

Additionally, OFAC sanctioned the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution, for facilitating Rwanda's support for the M23 movement and its political wing in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. This action aims to hold Rwanda accountable under the Washington Accords and pressure it to cease support for M23.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1.53 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $1,529,685. The settlement resolves potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of Russia sanctions.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to JSC Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian missile manufacturer majority-owned by the sanctioned state-owned defense company JSC Concern Almaz Antey. Although MMZA was not formally designated until 2022, it was considered blocked under OFAC's 50 Percent Rule during the relevant period.

OFAC determined the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. The Department of Justice also announced a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, under which the company will pay $975,721.84 in criminal penalties, with OFAC crediting $487,861 of this payment against its settlement.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended FAQs Regarding Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning the blocking and rejecting of transactions and the filing of reports with OFAC. This update aims to provide clearer guidance to financial institutions and other entities on their compliance obligations.

The amendments address various aspects of sanctions compliance, including procedures for handling blocked property and rejected transactions, as well as reporting requirements to OFAC. These updates are crucial for ensuring adherence to U.S. sanctions programs.
The issuance of amended FAQs reflects OFAC's ongoing commitment to providing comprehensive and up-to-date information to assist the public in understanding and complying with its regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Designations Removals, and New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. This action reflects a dynamic approach to sanctions policy, adjusting measures based on evolving geopolitical circumstances.

In conjunction with these updates, OFAC also issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions. These licenses aim to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions, while the updated FAQs offer further clarity on compliance requirements.

The designations and removals underscore the U.S. government's continuous evaluation of sanctions programs to ensure they remain effective in addressing national security and foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has implemented designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations target entities and individuals involved in activities that undermine American intellectual property rights.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses aim to mitigate unintended consequences and provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that might otherwise be prohibited.
The PAIPA designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to safeguarding American intellectual property and combating illicit activities that threaten economic security and innovation.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and an updated Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This action aims to refine existing sanctions measures and provide further clarity to stakeholders engaging with Venezuela.

The amended General License modifies previous authorizations, potentially impacting certain transactions or activities involving Venezuela. The accompanying FAQ offers additional guidance on the scope and application of these changes.

These adjustments reflect the U.S. government's ongoing review of its sanctions policies to ensure they remain targeted and effective in achieving foreign policy objectives while minimizing adverse impacts on legitimate activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities and a Cuban Bank, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a designation targeting Cuba. This action includes financial institutions, currency exchange firms, and energy and trading companies linked to Iran.

Specifically, Cuba's Banco International Commercial was designated due to its ties with Iran's Karafharin Bank, which has been under sanctions since 2020. The Iraq-based International Development Bank for Investment and Finance was also targeted for providing financial services and U.S. dollar access for Iran.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions, providing guidance on the scope of the new restrictions and potential authorizations for certain transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action indicates a targeted adjustment to the existing sanctions regime concerning Venezuela.

Designation removals can occur for various reasons, including a change in the designated party's behavior, a determination that the designation no longer serves U.S. foreign policy objectives, or a successful appeal by the designated entity.
Such removals are part of OFAC's ongoing process of reviewing and updating its sanctions lists to ensure they remain current and effective.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit networks that pose threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating international drug trafficking and terrorist financing by targeting key facilitators and organizations.
These measures typically result in the freezing of assets within U.S. jurisdiction and generally prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated parties.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined $1,529,685 by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,529,685 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This penalty resolves the company's potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of sanctions against Russia.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer. OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious.

In a coordinated action, the Department of Justice also announced a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, under which the company will pay $975,721.84 in criminal penalties. OFAC credited $487,861 of this payment against its settlement amount.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Pays $11,662,930 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has paid $11,662,930 to the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle 475 apparent violations of various sanctions programs. These violations occurred between September 18, 2021, and April 24, 2025, with a total transaction value of approximately $14.83 million.

The violations spanned multiple sanctions programs, including those related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. The conduct included payments via blocked banks, flaws in alert prioritization, delays in watchlist updates, and mishandling of accounts.

In a coordinated action, the U.S. Treasury Department also imposed a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN for anti-money laundering failures and a $750 million civil money penalty from the OCC, credited toward the FinCEN amount. OFAC classified the case as non-egregious, but noted aggravating factors such as recklessness, slow screening fixes, and inadequately trained staff.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has been assessed a civil penalty of $175,015 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement resolves apparent violations related to counter-narcotics screening and subpoena-response failures.

The penalty underscores the importance of robust compliance programs for freight forwarders and logistics companies to prevent facilitating illicit activities and ensure adherence to U.S. sanctions regulations.

OFAC continues to emphasize that companies must conduct thorough due diligence and implement effective screening procedures to identify and prevent transactions with sanctioned entities or individuals.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
